claims.claim: Cash flow is the increase or decrease in the amount of money a business, institution, or individual has — the amount of cash generated or consumed in a given time period (working definition attributed to CFI).
Money coming into a household is an inflow and money going out is an outflow; net cash flow is inflows minus outflows for the period.
When more money comes in than goes out over a period, the household has positive cash flow and its cash grows; when more goes out than comes in, it has negative cash flow and its cash shrinks.
Bill payment due dates often do not align with each other or with paychecks, and this misalignment is a common reason consumers fall behind on bills.
Missed or late payments are expensive and can make a tight money situation even tighter.

An overdraft occurs when there is not enough money in an account to cover a transaction and the bank or credit union pays it anyway; the account holder owes the amount overdrawn plus possible overdraft fees.
Overdraft fees vary, but many banks and credit unions charge $30 or more per transaction.
Filling out a spending tracker for at least two weeks — or even a month — gives a clearer picture of spending habits, and knowing what you spend on a monthly basis helps you pay bills on time.
A budget is the plan made in advance for how money should move; cash flow is the record of what actually happened, and knowing actual spending is what prepares a person to build a budget.
Cash flow is used to assess liquidity — how well a person or business can meet short-term obligations.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The term 'cash flow' is used loosely and can refer to several different measures.
positions: CFI notes that 'cash flow' can mean any of several things in finance — cash from operating activities, free cash flow variants, or the net change in cash — so the term must be clarified in context.

This lesson deliberately uses the plain household version (money moving into and out of a household over a period) and leaves the business cash-flow statement and its categories to the finance subject, referenced only.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is cash flow the same thing as a bank balance, or as tracking spending?
positions: A bank balance is a snapshot at one instant, while cash flow covers a period — both are real and answer different questions, so this lesson keeps them separate.
Tracking spending is the practice that produces the cash-flow numbers; the budget is the forward plan. The lesson teaches the distinction so the sibling budgeting topic can own the plan.

sourceRecords.title: Cash Flow
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Supports: cash flow as the increase or decrease in the amount of money a business, institution, or individual has — the cash generated or consumed in a given time period; cash flow used to assess liquidity (meeting short-term obligations); cash flow as the lifeblood of a company. sourceRecords.title: Know your overdraft options
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Supports: an overdraft occurs when there is not enough money in an account to cover a transaction and the bank or credit union pays it anyway, leaving the account holder to repay the amount plus possible overdraft fees; overdraft fees vary, with many banks and credit unions charging $30 or more per transaction; institutions cannot charge overdraft fees on ATM and one-time debit transactions unless the consumer opted in. Used for the cash-flow-problems section; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Track your spending with this easy tool
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21 (archived CFPB blog post by Courtney-Rose Dantus, June 11, 2019). Supports: filling out a spending tracker for at least two weeks — or even a month — to get a clearer picture of spending habits; knowing what you spend on a monthly basis helps you pay bills on time, get control of debt, and start saving; tracking actual spending is the step that prepares you to build a budget. Used for the tracking section and the cash-flow-versus-budget distinction; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Adjusting your bill due dates can help you stay on top of your bills and manage your cash flow
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21 (archived CFPB blog post by Irene Skricki, November 28, 2018). Supports: bill payment due dates often do not align with each other or with paychecks; CFPB research found many consumers struggle to pay bills on time and that misaligned due dates and income streams are a common reason people fall behind; missed or late payments are expensive and can make a tight money situation tighter; mapping bill due dates alongside the dates money comes in is the recommended first step. Used for the monthly-rhythm section and the honest consequences of cash-flow problems; no wording reproduced.
